L06 · Eigenvalue Decomposition

L06 · Eigenvalue Decomposition

Lecture 6 (slides "Eigenvalue Decomposition", 16 pages) · Deisenroth Ch. 4 · Strang Ch. 6

Lecture 6 slides (PDF) Revision notes: EVD via a photo filter Problem Set 6 (P3–P5 eigen) PSet 6 solutions Read them all on this page ↓

A square matrix can be understood through the directions it scales without turning. In order, this lecture covers: eigenvectors and eigenvalues, defined through the eigenvalue equation and the "only scaling" picture; how to compute them from the characteristic polynomial, with the vocabulary of eigenspectrum and eigenspace; the tutorial example; the eigen-decomposition A=QΛQ−1A=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}A=QΛQ−1; its interpretation as a change of basis, a scaling and a change back; the determinant as the product of the eigenvalues; the eigen-decomposition of the inverse; powers of a matrix; the meaning of a zero eigenvalue; and symmetric matrices with the spectral theorem. A clearly marked preview of quadratic forms, positive semi-definiteness and the SVD follows, because the previous two mid exams tested them.

Intuition: The photo filter (revision notes)

A photo filter moves each pixel at position xxx to SxSxSx, where S=[2112]S=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}S=[21​12​]; a round logo becomes a tilted oval. Follow three pixels:
S[10]=[21],S[11]=[33]=3[11],S[1−1]=[1−1]=1[1−1].S\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad S\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\3\end{bmatrix}=3\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad S\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}=1\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}.S[10​]=[21​],S[11​]=[33​]=3[11​],S[1−1​]=[1−1​]=1[1−1​].
The first pixel is pushed off its line, but two special directions are not tilted at all: the diagonal is stretched by a factor of 333, and the anti-diagonal is left unchanged. These directions are the eigenvectors, and 333 and 111 are the eigenvalues. Everything about SSS — how it scales area, how to undo it, what happens when it is applied repeatedly — follows from them.

#1. Eigenvectors and eigenvalues

🧩Background you needmultiples of a vector, and 'staying on the same line'

A scalar multiple of a vector points along the same line: 3 (1,2)=(3,6)3\,(1,2)=(3,6)3(1,2)=(3,6) is three times as long in the same direction, and −1 (1,2)=(−1,−2)-1\,(1,2)=(-1,-2)−1(1,2)=(−1,−2) points the opposite way along the same line.

Most vectors get turned by a matrix. With A=[2112]A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}A=[21​12​],
A[10]=[21],A\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix},A[10​]=[21​],
which points in a different direction from (1,0)(1,0)(1,0).

A few special vectors only get stretched.
A[11]=[33]=3[11].A\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\3\end{bmatrix}=3\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.A[11​]=[33​]=3[11​].
The output is just 333 times the input. Such a vector is an eigenvector, and the stretch factor 333 is its eigenvalue. "Eigen" is German for "own" — these are the matrix's own special directions.

Definition: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues

For square matrices, eigenvectors and eigenvalues are the vectors and numbers that make up the eigen-decomposition of a matrix; they reveal its structure. For A∈Rn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}A∈Rn×n, a vector q∈Rnq\in\mathbb{R}^nq∈Rn with q≠0q\neq\mathbf 0q=0 is an eigenvector of AAA if
Aq=λq(the eigenvalue equation)Aq=\lambda q\qquad(\text{the eigenvalue equation})Aq=λq(the eigenvalue equation)
for some number λ\lambdaλ, which is called the eigenvalue of AAA associated with qqq.

The linear-transformation picture. Feeding qqq into the system AAA returns λq\lambda qλq: the action is only scaling. Geometrically, AqAqAq lies on the same line through the origin as qqq. Along that line AAA stretches (if ∣λ∣>1|\lambda|>1∣λ∣>1), shrinks (if ∣λ∣<1|\lambda|<1∣λ∣<1), flips (if λ<0\lambda<0λ<0) or squashes to the origin (if λ=0\lambda=0λ=0) — but it never moves a point off the line.

Three remarks on the definition:

  • The condition q≠0q\neq\mathbf 0q=0 matters, because A0=λ0A\mathbf 0=\lambda\mathbf 0A0=λ0 holds for every λ\lambdaλ and says nothing.
  • Eigenvectors are defined only up to scale, since A(cq)=c Aq=λ(cq)A(cq)=c\,Aq=\lambda(cq)A(cq)=cAq=λ(cq). What matters is the direction; we usually normalise to ∥q∥2=1\|q\|_2=1∥q∥2​=1, and even then the sign is free.
  • Only square matrices have eigenvalues, because AqAqAq and qqq must live in the same space.

For example, (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) is not an eigenvector of SSS, since S(0,1)⊤=(1,2)⊤S(0,1)^\top=(1,2)^\topS(0,1)⊤=(1,2)⊤ is not a multiple of (0,1)(0,1)(0,1); but (−2,−2)(-2,-2)(−2,−2) is, since S(−2,−2)⊤=(−6,−6)⊤=3 (−2,−2)⊤S(-2,-2)^\top=(-6,-6)^\top=3\,(-2,-2)^\topS(−2,−2)⊤=(−6,−6)⊤=3(−2,−2)⊤.

Remember

An eigenvector is a non-zero direction that AAA only scales: Aq=λqAq=\lambda qAq=λq.

#2. Computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors

🧩Background you needdeterminants, quadratic equations, and why det(A − λI) = 0

The 2×2 determinant

det⁡[abcd]=ad−bc.Example: det⁡[3142]=3⋅2−1⋅4=2.\det\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}=ad-bc .\qquad\text{Example: }\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\4&2\end{bmatrix}=3\cdot2-1\cdot4=2 .det[ac​bd​]=ad−bc.Example: det[34​12​]=3⋅2−1⋅4=2.

Subtracting λI\lambda IλI

λI\lambda IλI is the identity matrix scaled by λ\lambdaλ, so subtracting it takes λ\lambdaλ away from the diagonal entries only:
A−λI=[2112]−[λ00λ]=[2−λ112−λ].A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\lambda&0\\0&\lambda\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2-\lambda&1\\1&2-\lambda\end{bmatrix}.A−λI=[21​12​]−[λ0​0λ​]=[2−λ1​12−λ​].

Solving a quadratic equation

To solve λ2−4λ+3=0\lambda^2-4\lambda+3=0λ2−4λ+3=0, look for two numbers that multiply to 333 and add to −4-4−4: they are −1-1−1 and −3-3−3. So (λ−1)(λ−3)=0(\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)=0(λ−1)(λ−3)=0, and the solutions are λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 and λ=3\lambda=3λ=3. If you cannot spot the factors, use the formula
λ=4±42−4⋅1⋅32=4±22∈{1,3}.\lambda=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{4^2-4\cdot1\cdot3}}{2}=\frac{4\pm2}{2}\in\{1,3\}.λ=24±42−4⋅1⋅3​​=24±2​∈{1,3}.

Why we need det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(A-\lambda I)=0det(A−λI)=0

We want a non-zero vector qqq with (A−λI)q=0(A-\lambda I)q=\mathbf 0(A−λI)q=0 — that is, the matrix A−λIA-\lambda IA−λI must squash some non-zero vector to zero. From L02, a matrix does that exactly when it is singular, i.e. when its determinant is 000. So the eigenvalues are precisely the values of λ\lambdaλ that make det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(A-\lambda I)=0det(A−λI)=0.

Move everything to one side of the eigenvalue equation, writing λq=λIq\lambda q=\lambda Iqλq=λIq:
Aq=λq⟹Aq−λIq=0⟹(A−λI) q=0.Aq=\lambda q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Aq-\lambda Iq=\mathbf 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (A-\lambda I)\,q=\mathbf 0 .Aq=λq⟹Aq−λIq=0⟹(A−λI)q=0.
We want a non-zero qqq that A−λIA-\lambda IA−λI sends to zero. If A−λIA-\lambda IA−λI were invertible, the only solution would be q=(A−λI)−10=0q=(A-\lambda I)^{-1}\mathbf 0=\mathbf 0q=(A−λI)−10=0. So a non-zero solution exists exactly when A−λIA-\lambda IA−λI is singular, that is, when
p(λ)=det⁡(A−λI)=0.p(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda I)=0 .p(λ)=det(A−λI)=0.
The function ppp is the characteristic polynomial of AAA, and it has degree nnn. (The slide writes det⁡(Aq−λq)\det(Aq-\lambda q)det(Aq−λq) as shorthand; the determinant is that of the matrix A−λIA-\lambda IA−λI.)

The vocabulary:

  • AAA has nnn eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_nλ1​,…,λn​ (the roots of ppp, counted with multiplicity) and correspondingly nnn eigenvectors.
  • The eigenspectrum (or spectrum) is the set of eigenvalues.
  • The eigenspace is the span of the eigenvectors; for a particular λ\lambdaλ it is N(A−λI)\mathcal N(A-\lambda I)N(A−λI), the null space of L03.
Definition: The recipe
  1. Write down A−λIA-\lambda IA−λI, subtracting λ\lambdaλ from the diagonal entries only.
  2. Compute p(λ)=det⁡(A−λI)p(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda I)p(λ)=det(A−λI). For a 2×22\times22×2 matrix there is a shortcut:
    p(λ)=λ2−(a+d) λ+(ad−bc)=λ2−tr⁡(A) λ+det⁡A.p(\lambda)=\lambda^2-(a+d)\,\lambda+(ad-bc)=\lambda^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)\,\lambda+\det A .p(λ)=λ2−(a+d)λ+(ad−bc)=λ2−tr(A)λ+detA.
  3. Solve p(λ)=0p(\lambda)=0p(λ)=0.
  4. For each eigenvalue λi\lambda_iλi​, solve (A−λiI)q=0(A-\lambda_iI)q=\mathbf 0(A−λi​I)q=0. One row is enough: the other rows are multiples of it, precisely because we chose λi\lambda_iλi​ to make the matrix singular.
  5. Choose a simple qqq, normalise it, and check that Aq=λqAq=\lambda qAq=λq.

Two sanity checks: ∑iλi=tr⁡A\sum_i\lambda_i=\operatorname{tr}A∑i​λi​=trA and ∏iλi=det⁡A\prod_i\lambda_i=\det A∏i​λi​=detA.

Worked example: The slide's tutorial problem: A=[4−2−21]A=\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-2&1\end{bmatrix}A=[4−2​−21​]

Step 1 — the characteristic polynomial.
det⁡(A−λI)=det⁡[4−λ−2−21−λ]=(4−λ)(1−λ)−(−2)(−2)=(λ2−5λ+4)−4=λ2−5λ.\det(A-\lambda I)=\det\begin{bmatrix}4-\lambda&-2\\-2&1-\lambda\end{bmatrix} =(4-\lambda)(1-\lambda)-(-2)(-2) =(\lambda^2-5\lambda+4)-4 =\lambda^2-5\lambda .det(A−λI)=det[4−λ−2​−21−λ​]=(4−λ)(1−λ)−(−2)(−2)=(λ2−5λ+4)−4=λ2−5λ.
Step 2 — the eigenvalues. λ2−5λ=λ(λ−5)=0\lambda^2-5\lambda=\lambda(\lambda-5)=0λ2−5λ=λ(λ−5)=0 gives λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0 and λ2=5\lambda_2=5λ2​=5. As a check, 0+5=5=tr⁡A0+5=5=\operatorname{tr}A0+5=5=trA and 0⋅5=0=det⁡A0\cdot5=0=\det A0⋅5=0=detA.

Step 3 — the eigenvector for λ=0\lambda=0λ=0. Solve (A−0I)v=0(A-0I)v=\mathbf 0(A−0I)v=0:
[4−2−21][v1v2]=[00].\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-2&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}v_1\\v_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}.[4−2​−21​][v1​v2​​]=[00​].
The second row gives v2=2v1v_2=2v_1v2​=2v1​, and substituting into the first row gives 4v1−2(2v1)=04v_1-2(2v_1)=04v1​−2(2v1​)=0, which is consistent. Hence v=v1(1,2)v=v_1(1,2)v=v1​(1,2), with ∥v∥=v15\|v\|=v_1\sqrt5∥v∥=v1​5​; choosing v1=1/5v_1=1/\sqrt5v1​=1/5​,
v1=15[12].\mathbf v_1=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}.v1​=5​1​[12​].
Step 4 — the eigenvector for λ=5\lambda=5λ=5 (completing the slide). Here
A−5I=[−1−2−2−4],A-5I=\begin{bmatrix}-1&-2\\-2&-4\end{bmatrix},A−5I=[−1−2​−2−4​],
and the first row gives v1=−2v2v_1=-2v_2v1​=−2v2​, so
v2=15[−21].\mathbf v_2=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}-2\\1\end{bmatrix}.v2​=5​1​[−21​].
Check. A(−2,1)⊤=(−10,5)⊤=5 (−2,1)⊤A(-2,1)^\top=(-10,5)^\top=5\,(-2,1)^\topA(−2,1)⊤=(−10,5)⊤=5(−2,1)⊤. Moreover v1⊤v2=0\mathbf v_1^\top\mathbf v_2=0v1⊤​v2​=0, as it must be for a symmetric matrix. Note that λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 means AAA is singular: column 1 is −2-2−2 times column 2.

λ=3: [−111−1]v=0 ⇒ v2=v1,q1=12[11];λ=1: [1111]v=0 ⇒ v2=−v1,q2=12[−11].\lambda=3:\ \begin{bmatrix}-1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}v=\mathbf 0\ \Rightarrow\ v_2=v_1,\quad q_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}; \qquad \lambda=1:\ \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}v=\mathbf 0\ \Rightarrow\ v_2=-v_1,\quad q_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}.λ=3: [−11​1−1​]v=0 ⇒ v2​=v1​,q1​=2​1​[11​];λ=1: [11​11​]v=0 ⇒ v2​=−v1​,q2​=2​1​[−11​].

PSet 6, Problem 3. For A=[1423]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\2&3\end{bmatrix}A=[12​43​], p(λ)=λ2−4λ−5=(λ−5)(λ+1)p(\lambda)=\lambda^2-4\lambda-5=(\lambda-5)(\lambda+1)p(λ)=λ2−4λ−5=(λ−5)(λ+1), with eigenvectors (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) and (−2,1)(-2,1)(−2,1). These are not orthogonal, because AAA is not symmetric.

🔍Where does this come from?the shortcut λ2−tr⁡(A) λ+det⁡A\lambda^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)\,\lambda+\det Aλ2−tr(A)λ+detA

Expand the determinant for a general 2×22\times22×2 matrix:
det⁡[a−λbcd−λ]=(a−λ)(d−λ)−bc=λ2−(a+d)λ+(ad−bc).\det\begin{bmatrix}a-\lambda&b\\c&d-\lambda\end{bmatrix}=(a-\lambda)(d-\lambda)-bc=\lambda^2-(a+d)\lambda+(ad-bc).det[a−λc​bd−λ​]=(a−λ)(d−λ)−bc=λ2−(a+d)λ+(ad−bc).
The middle coefficient a+da+da+d is the trace (sum of the diagonal) and the last term ad−bcad-bcad−bc is the determinant. So you can write the polynomial down without expanding anything.

Bonus. If the roots are λ1,λ2\lambda_1,\lambda_2λ1​,λ2​, then λ2−(λ1+λ2)λ+λ1λ2\lambda^2-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\lambda+\lambda_1\lambda_2λ2−(λ1​+λ2​)λ+λ1​λ2​ is the same polynomial, so comparing coefficients gives λ1+λ2=tr⁡A\lambda_1+\lambda_2=\operatorname{tr}Aλ1​+λ2​=trA and λ1λ2=det⁡A\lambda_1\lambda_2=\det Aλ1​λ2​=detA — the two sanity checks in the recipe.

Remember

Solve det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(A-\lambda I)=0det(A−λI)=0 for the eigenvalues, then (A−λI)q=0(A-\lambda I)q=\mathbf 0(A−λI)q=0 for each eigenvector, and check the results against the trace and the determinant.

#3. The eigen-decomposition A=QΛQ−1A=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}A=QΛQ−1

🧩Background you needmultiplying by a diagonal matrix

On the right, a diagonal matrix scales the columns.
[1234][50010]=[1⋅52⋅103⋅54⋅10]=[5201540]:\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5&0\\0&10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot5&2\cdot10\\3\cdot5&4\cdot10\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5&20\\15&40\end{bmatrix}:[13​24​][50​010​]=[1⋅53⋅5​2⋅104⋅10​]=[515​2040​]:
column 1 was multiplied by 555 and column 2 by 101010.

On the left, it scales the rows instead. You only need the column version here.

Putting columns side by side. Writing Q=[ q1 q2 ]Q=[\,q_1\ q_2\,]Q=[q1​ q2​] means "the matrix whose first column is q1q_1q1​ and second column is q2q_2q2​". Then AQ=[ Aq1 Aq2 ]AQ=[\,Aq_1\ Aq_2\,]AQ=[Aq1​ Aq2​], because each column of a product is AAA times the corresponding column (L02).

Write the nnn eigenvalue equations side by side,
Aq1=λ1q1,Aq2=λ2q2,…,Aqn=λnqn,Aq_1=\lambda_1q_1,\quad Aq_2=\lambda_2q_2,\quad\dots,\quad Aq_n=\lambda_nq_n,Aq1​=λ1​q1​,Aq2​=λ2​q2​,…,Aqn​=λn​qn​,
and collect the eigenvectors as the columns of QQQ and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of Λ\LambdaΛ:
Q=[(q1)1(q2)1⋯(qn)1(q1)2(q2)2⋯(qn)2⋮⋮⋱⋮(q1)n(q2)n⋯(qn)n]=[ q1 q2 ⋯ qn ],Λ=[λ10⋯00λ2⋯0⋮⋮⋱⋮00⋯λn].Q=\begin{bmatrix}(q_1)_1&(q_2)_1&\cdots&(q_n)_1\\(q_1)_2&(q_2)_2&\cdots&(q_n)_2\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\(q_1)_n&(q_2)_n&\cdots&(q_n)_n\end{bmatrix}=\big[\,q_1\ q_2\ \cdots\ q_n\,\big], \qquad \Lambda=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda_1&0&\cdots&0\\0&\lambda_2&\cdots&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&\lambda_n\end{bmatrix}.Q=​(q1​)1​(q1​)2​⋮(q1​)n​​(q2​)1​(q2​)2​⋮(q2​)n​​⋯⋯⋱⋯​(qn​)1​(qn​)2​⋮(qn​)n​​​=[q1​ q2​ ⋯ qn​],Λ=​λ1​0⋮0​0λ2​⋮0​⋯⋯⋱⋯​00⋮λn​​​.
Column iii of AQAQAQ is AqiAq_iAqi​, and column iii of QΛQ\LambdaQΛ is λiqi\lambda_iq_iλi​qi​ (multiplying by a diagonal matrix on the right scales the columns). So all nnn equations together say
AQ=QΛ,AQ=Q\Lambda ,AQ=QΛ,
and multiplying on the right by Q−1Q^{-1}Q−1 gives the eigen-decomposition (EVD):
  A=QΛQ−1  \boxed{\;A=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}\;}A=QΛQ−1​
The last step requires QQQ to be invertible, that is, the eigenvectors must be linearly independent. This always holds for symmetric matrices (§9), and also whenever the nnn eigenvalues are distinct.

Worked example: Decompositions of the two filters

For the photo filter,
S=12[1−111]⏟Q[3001]⏟Λ12[11−11]⏟Q−1=Q⊤.S=\underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}}_{Q} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}}_{\Lambda} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}}_{Q^{-1}=Q^\top}.S=Q2​1​[11​−11​]​​Λ[30​01​]​​Q−1=Q⊤2​1​[1−1​11​]​​.
Multiplying out confirms it:
QΛQ⊤=12[3−131][11−11]=12[4224]=[2112]=S.Q\Lambda Q^\top=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\3&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}=S .QΛQ⊤=21​[33​−11​][1−1​11​]=21​[42​24​]=[21​12​]=S.
For the practice filter, with the eigenvalues ordered (4,−1)(4,-1)(4,−1),
M=15[211−2][400−1]15[211−2],M=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&-2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&-2\end{bmatrix},M=5​1​[21​1−2​][40​0−1​]5​1​[21​1−2​],
where here Q−1=Q⊤=QQ^{-1}=Q^\top=QQ−1=Q⊤=Q. Listing the eigenvalues in a different order swaps the columns of QQQ along with them: what matters is the pairing of each λi\lambda_iλi​ with its qiq_iqi​.

🔍Where does this come from?why AQ=QΛAQ=Q\LambdaAQ=QΛ, column by column

Compute both sides one column at a time.

Left side. Column iii of AQAQAQ is AqiAq_iAqi​. Because qiq_iqi​ is an eigenvector, Aqi=λiqiAq_i=\lambda_iq_iAqi​=λi​qi​.

Right side. Column iii of QΛQ\LambdaQΛ is column iii of QQQ scaled by the iii-th diagonal entry of Λ\LambdaΛ, which is λiqi\lambda_iq_iλi​qi​.

Every column agrees, so AQ=QΛAQ=Q\LambdaAQ=QΛ. If QQQ has an inverse, multiply both sides on the right by Q−1Q^{-1}Q−1:
AQQ−1=QΛQ−1⟹A=QΛQ−1.AQQ^{-1}=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad A=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}.AQQ−1=QΛQ−1⟹A=QΛQ−1.

Remember

AQ=QΛAQ=Q\LambdaAQ=QΛ gives A=QΛQ−1A=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}A=QΛQ−1, with the eigenvectors as the columns of QQQ and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of Λ\LambdaΛ, in the same order.

#4. What the EVD reveals: change of basis → scaling → change back

🧩Background you needwhat 'change of basis' means

Coordinates depend on your axes. The point (1,0)(1,0)(1,0) on ordinary axes can also be described using the tilted axes q1=12(1,1)q_1=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,1)q1​=2​1​(1,1) and q2=12(−1,1)q_2=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(-1,1)q2​=2​1​(−1,1). In those axes it is 12\tfrac1{\sqrt2}2​1​ along q1q_1q1​ and −12-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}−2​1​ along q2q_2q2​:
12q1−12q2=12[11]−12[−11]=[10].\frac{1}{\sqrt2}q_1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}q_2=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}-\frac12\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}.2​1​q1​−2​1​q2​=21​[11​]−21​[−11​]=[10​].
"Change of basis" just means re-describing the same point using different axes. Q−1xQ^{-1}xQ−1x gives the new description; QQQ converts back.

Why choose the eigenvector axes? Along those axes the matrix does nothing but stretch — no turning — so its action is as simple as possible.

x∈Rn ⟶  Q−1  ⟶  Λ  ⟶  Q  ⟶ Axx\in\mathbb{R}^n\ \longrightarrow\ \boxed{\ Q^{-1}\ }\ \longrightarrow\ \boxed{\ \Lambda\ }\ \longrightarrow\ \boxed{\ Q\ }\ \longrightarrow\ Axx∈Rn ⟶  Q−1 ​ ⟶  Λ ​ ⟶  Q ​ ⟶ Ax
The three boxes are a transformation (change of basis), a scaling (in the new basis) and an inverse transformation (change of basis back). Reading Ax=QΛQ−1xAx=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}xAx=QΛQ−1x from right to left:

  1. c=Q−1xc=Q^{-1}xc=Q−1x gives the coordinates of xxx in the eigenbasis, so that x=Qc=∑iciqix=Qc=\sum_ic_iq_ix=Qc=∑i​ci​qi​;
  2. Λc\Lambda cΛc scales coordinate iii by λi\lambda_iλi​, each coordinate separately, with no mixing;
  3. Q(Λc)=∑iλiciqiQ(\Lambda c)=\sum_i\lambda_ic_iq_iQ(Λc)=∑i​λi​ci​qi​ converts back to standard coordinates.

In a single formula:
Ax=∑i=1nλi ci qiwherex=∑i=1nci qi.Ax=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\,c_i\,q_i\qquad\text{where}\qquad x=\sum_{i=1}^nc_i\,q_i .Ax=i=1∑n​λi​ci​qi​wherex=i=1∑n​ci​qi​.
A matrix that looks complicated in the standard basis is only scaling in its eigenbasis.

The visualisation (slide p11). A unit circle carrying the vectors q1,q2q_1,q_2q1​,q2​ is mapped by AAA directly to an ellipse with axes λ1q1\lambda_1q_1λ1​q1​ and λ2q2\lambda_2q_2λ2​q2​. Going the long way round, Q−1Q^{-1}Q−1 turns q1,q2q_1,q_2q1​,q2​ onto e1,e2e_1,e_2e1​,e2​; Λ\LambdaΛ stretches the circle into an ellipse aligned with the axes, λ1e1\lambda_1e_1λ1​e1​ and λ2e2\lambda_2e_2λ2​e2​; and QQQ turns it back. Both routes produce the same ellipse.

#5. Determinant in terms of eigenvalues

🧩Background you needthe product rule for determinants

The rule: det⁡(AB)=det⁡(A) det⁡(B)\det(AB)=\det(A)\,\det(B)det(AB)=det(A)det(B) — the area-scaling of "do BBB, then AAA" is the product of the two scalings.

A consequence: since Q−1Q=IQ^{-1}Q=IQ−1Q=I and det⁡I=1\det I=1detI=1, we get det⁡(Q−1)det⁡(Q)=1\det(Q^{-1})\det(Q)=1det(Q−1)det(Q)=1, so det⁡(Q−1)=1det⁡Q\det(Q^{-1})=\dfrac{1}{\det Q}det(Q−1)=detQ1​.

The determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of the diagonal entries: det⁡[3005]=15\det\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&5\end{bmatrix}=15det[30​05​]=15. Geometrically it stretches one axis by 333 and the other by 555, so areas grow by 151515.

Using det⁡(BC)=det⁡B det⁡C\det(BC)=\det B\,\det Cdet(BC)=detBdetC, det⁡(Q−1)=1/det⁡Q\det(Q^{-1})=1/\det Qdet(Q−1)=1/detQ, and the fact that the determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of its diagonal entries,
det⁡(A)=det⁡(QΛQ−1)=det⁡(Q) det⁡(Λ) det⁡(Q−1)=det⁡(Q)(∏i=1nλi)1det⁡(Q)=∏i=1nλi.\det(A)=\det(Q\Lambda Q^{-1})=\det(Q)\,\det(\Lambda)\,\det(Q^{-1})=\det(Q)\Big(\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\Big)\frac{1}{\det(Q)}=\prod_{i=1}^n\lambda_i .det(A)=det(QΛQ−1)=det(Q)det(Λ)det(Q−1)=det(Q)(i=1∏n​λi​)det(Q)1​=i=1∏n​λi​.
If one of the eigenvalues is zero, the determinant of the matrix is zero.

Connecting this with the meaning of the determinant (as the slide encourages). ∣det⁡A∣|\det A|∣detA∣ is the factor by which AAA scales area or volume. In the eigenbasis, AAA stretches axis iii by λi\lambda_iλi​, so a unit box becomes a box of volume ∏iλi\prod_i\lambda_i∏i​λi​, and the changes of basis Q−1Q^{-1}Q−1 and QQQ cancel. For the photo filter, det⁡S=3=3⋅1\det S=3=3\cdot1detS=3=3⋅1, so the logo's area grows from π\piπ to 3π3\pi3π. For the practice filter, det⁡M=−4=4⋅(−1)\det M=-4=4\cdot(-1)detM=−4=4⋅(−1): areas grow fourfold, and the minus sign records the flip. Applying SSS twice multiplies areas by 999.

In the same way, tr⁡(A)=∑iλi\operatorname{tr}(A)=\sum_i\lambda_itr(A)=∑i​λi​; for a 2×22\times22×2 matrix this can be read directly from p(λ)=λ2−tr⁡(A) λ+det⁡Ap(\lambda)=\lambda^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)\,\lambda+\det Ap(λ)=λ2−tr(A)λ+detA.

#6. EVD of the inverse

A−1A^{-1}A−1 has the same eigenvectors as AAA, with eigenvalues 1/λi1/\lambda_i1/λi​. Assume AAA is invertible, so that every eigenvalue is non-zero, and multiply the eigenvalue equation by A−1A^{-1}A−1:
Aq=λq⟹A−1Aq=λ A−1q⟹A−1q=1λ q.Aq=\lambda q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A^{-1}Aq=\lambda\,A^{-1}q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A^{-1}q=\frac{1}{\lambda}\,q .Aq=λq⟹A−1Aq=λA−1q⟹A−1q=λ1​q.
So qqq is an eigenvector of A−1A^{-1}A−1 with eigenvalue 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ. In matrix form,
A−1=(QΛQ−1)−1=QΛ−1Q−1,Λ−1=diag⁡(1/λ1,…,1/λn).A^{-1}=\big(Q\Lambda Q^{-1}\big)^{-1}=Q\Lambda^{-1}Q^{-1},\qquad \Lambda^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}\big(1/\lambda_1,\dots,1/\lambda_n\big).A−1=(QΛQ−1)−1=QΛ−1Q−1,Λ−1=diag(1/λ1​,…,1/λn​).

#7. Powers of a matrix

🧩Background you needpowers of a diagonal matrix

A diagonal matrix multiplied by itself just squares the diagonal entries:
[3002]2=[3002][3002]=[9004],[3002]k=[3k002k].\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}^2=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}9&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix},\qquad \begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}^k=\begin{bmatrix}3^k&0\\0&2^k\end{bmatrix}.[30​02​]2=[30​02​][30​02​]=[90​04​],[30​02​]k=[3k0​02k​].
That is why the eigen-decomposition is so useful for powers: it turns the hard problem (AkA^kAk) into the easy one (Λk\Lambda^kΛk).

A2=AA=QΛQ−1Q⏟= IΛQ−1=QΛ2Q−1,and in generalAn=QΛnQ−1,Λn=diag⁡(λ1n,…,λnn).A^2=AA=Q\Lambda\underbrace{Q^{-1}Q}_{=\,I}\Lambda Q^{-1}=Q\Lambda^2Q^{-1}, \qquad\text{and in general}\qquad A^n=Q\Lambda^nQ^{-1},\quad \Lambda^n=\operatorname{diag}\big(\lambda_1^n,\dots,\lambda_n^n\big).A2=AA=QΛ=IQ−1Q​​ΛQ−1=QΛ2Q−1,and in generalAn=QΛnQ−1,Λn=diag(λ1n​,…,λnn​).
Connecting this with the linear-transformation picture (as the slide encourages). Applying AAA kkk times means going round the loop kkk times; each inner Q−1QQ^{-1}QQ−1Q cancels, so we change basis once, scale kkk times, and change back once.

More generally, any polynomial f(A)=c0I+c1A+c2A2+⋯f(A)=c_0I+c_1A+c_2A^2+\cdotsf(A)=c0​I+c1​A+c2​A2+⋯ has the same eigenvectors as AAA, with eigenvalues f(λi)f(\lambda_i)f(λi​); a term A−1A^{-1}A−1 contributes 1/λi1/\lambda_i1/λi​. In particular, adding cIcIcI shifts every eigenvalue by ccc: in PSet 6, Problem 3, A+IA+IA+I has eigenvalues 666 and 000, so A+IA+IA+I is singular.

#8. Zero eigenvalues ⇔ dependent columns

Suppose λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 is an eigenvalue with eigenvector q≠0q\neq\mathbf 0q=0. Then
Aq=λq=0.Aq=\lambda q=\mathbf 0 .Aq=λq=0.
Since AqAqAq is the combination of the columns of AAA with weights given by the entries of qqq — not all of them zero — we have found a non-trivial combination of the columns equal to zero. By definition, the columns of AAA are linearly dependent.

Theorem / Key result: Four equivalent facts

For a square matrix AAA:
0 is an eigenvalue  ⟺  the columns are dependent  ⟺  det⁡A=0  ⟺  A has no inverse.0\ \text{is an eigenvalue}\iff\text{the columns are dependent}\iff\det A=0\iff A\ \text{has no inverse}.0 is an eigenvalue⟺the columns are dependent⟺detA=0⟺A has no inverse.
A negative eigenvalue is harmless, since a flip can be undone; only a zero eigenvalue loses information.

Worked example: The flatten filter

F=Q[1000]Q⊤=12[1111]F=Q\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}Q^\top=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}F=Q[10​00​]Q⊤=21​[11​11​]
has two identical columns, and its eigenvector (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1) is exactly the recipe for the dependence, −a1+a2=0-a_1+a_2=\mathbf 0−a1​+a2​=0. Its determinant is 14−14=0\tfrac14-\tfrac14=041​−41​=0. The pixels (1,0)(1,0)(1,0) and (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) both land on (12,12)(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)(21​,21​), so the original photo cannot be recovered and no inverse exists. And Fk=FF^k=FFk=F: flattening twice is the same as flattening once.

The link with L05: redundant features give X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X a zero eigenvalue, which is why it becomes singular. In 2024 MCQ 20, a zero eigenvalue implies dependent columns and a zero determinant, and the matrix is not invertible.

Remember

λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 means some non-zero qqq is sent to 0\mathbf 00: the columns are dependent, det⁡=0\det=0det=0, and there is no inverse.

#9. Symmetric matrices — the spectral theorem

🧩Background you needorthogonal matrices, recapped

An orthogonal matrix QQQ has columns that are perpendicular to each other and each of length 111 (L02). Then Q⊤Q=IQ^\top Q=IQ⊤Q=I, so its inverse is simply its transpose: Q−1=Q⊤Q^{-1}=Q^\topQ−1=Q⊤. No calculation needed — just flip the matrix.

Geometrically, an orthogonal matrix is a rotation (or a reflection): it turns the plane without stretching or squashing anything.

So for a symmetric matrix, A=QΛQ⊤A=Q\Lambda Q^\topA=QΛQ⊤ says: rotate, stretch along perpendicular axes, rotate back.

Theorem / Key result: The spectral theorem

For a symmetric matrix A∈Rn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}A∈Rn×n there exists an orthonormal basis of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn consisting of eigenvectors of AAA, and every eigenvalue is real. Consequently Q⊤Q=IQ^\top Q=IQ⊤Q=I, so Q−1=Q⊤Q^{-1}=Q^\topQ−1=Q⊤ (QQQ is an orthonormal matrix), and
  A=QΛQ⊤  \boxed{\;A=Q\Lambda Q^\top\;}A=QΛQ⊤​

Derivation: Why Q−1=Q⊤Q^{-1}=Q^\topQ−1=Q⊤ fits with symmetry (slide p16)

Transposing A=QΛQ−1A=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}A=QΛQ−1, and using Λ⊤=Λ\Lambda^\top=\LambdaΛ⊤=Λ, gives
A⊤=(Q−1)⊤Λ Q⊤.A^\top=\big(Q^{-1}\big)^\top\Lambda\,Q^\top .A⊤=(Q−1)⊤ΛQ⊤.
Since A=A⊤A=A^\topA=A⊤, the two expressions describe the same matrix, and choosing Q−1=Q⊤Q^{-1}=Q^\topQ−1=Q⊤ makes them identical term by term. The spectral theorem guarantees that this choice is always available.

Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal. Let Aq1=λ1q1Aq_1=\lambda_1q_1Aq1​=λ1​q1​ and Aq2=λ2q2Aq_2=\lambda_2q_2Aq2​=λ2​q2​ with λ1≠λ2\lambda_1\neq\lambda_2λ1​=λ2​. Then
λ1 q1⊤q2=(Aq1)⊤q2=q1⊤A⊤q2=q1⊤Aq2=λ2 q1⊤q2,\lambda_1\,q_1^\top q_2=(Aq_1)^\top q_2=q_1^\top A^\top q_2=q_1^\top Aq_2=\lambda_2\,q_1^\top q_2 ,λ1​q1⊤​q2​=(Aq1​)⊤q2​=q1⊤​A⊤q2​=q1⊤​Aq2​=λ2​q1⊤​q2​,
so (λ1−λ2) q1⊤q2=0(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)\,q_1^\top q_2=0(λ1​−λ2​)q1⊤​q2​=0, and therefore q1⊤q2=0q_1^\top q_2=0q1⊤​q2​=0.

In summary, a symmetric matrix has orthonormal eigenvectors and real eigenvalues. Geometrically it acts by rotating (the orthonormal Q⊤Q^\topQ⊤), stretching along perpendicular axes (Λ\LambdaΛ), and rotating back (QQQ), so it always maps the unit circle to a clean ellipse whose axes point along the eigenvectors.

Worked example: Badly behaved, non-symmetric matrices

The matrix
L=[3011]L=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix}L=[31​01​]
has the same eigenvalues as SSS, namely 333 and 111, but its eigenvectors (2,1)(2,1)(2,1) and (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) are not perpendicular. It still has a decomposition,
L=QΛQ−1,Q=[2011],Q−1=12[10−12]≠Q⊤,L=Q\Lambda Q^{-1},\qquad Q=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad Q^{-1}=\frac12\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-1&2\end{bmatrix}\neq Q^\top ,L=QΛQ−1,Q=[21​01​],Q−1=21​[1−1​02​]=Q⊤,
but its change of basis is a skew rather than a rotation.

The rotation by 90∘90^\circ90∘, R=[0−110]R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}R=[01​−10​], has characteristic polynomial λ2+1\lambda^2+1λ2+1, which has no real roots: every direction is turned, and none is merely scaled. Symmetry is what guarantees real eigenvalues.

In 2025 MCQ 15, for symmetric AAA: the eigenvalues are real (true); eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal (true); A=QΛQ⊤A=Q\Lambda Q^\topA=QΛQ⊤ with orthonormal QQQ (true); "AAA cannot be diagonalised by an orthogonal matrix" (false). In 2024 MCQ 15: A⊤=AA^\top=AA⊤=A (true); "AAA must be diagonal" (false); real eigenvalues (true); orthogonal eigenvectors (true).

Remember

A symmetric matrix satisfies A=QΛQ⊤A=Q\Lambda Q^\topA=QΛQ⊤ with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors: rotate, stretch, rotate back.

#10. Preview: quadratic forms, PSD, SVD (outline Week 6; tested in 2024/2025 mids)

The 2026 slides so far end with the spectral theorem. The outline's Week 6 continues with the topics below, and both previous mid exams tested them, so it is worth knowing at least these facts.

Quadratic forms and definiteness. For a symmetric matrix, substituting A=QΛQ⊤A=Q\Lambda Q^\topA=QΛQ⊤ gives
x⊤Ax=x⊤QΛQ⊤x=∑i=1nλi (qi⊤x)2.x^\top Ax=x^\top Q\Lambda Q^\top x=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\,\big(q_i^\top x\big)^2 .x⊤Ax=x⊤QΛQ⊤x=i=1∑n​λi​(qi⊤​x)2.
It follows that:

  • AAA is positive semi-definite (PSD) exactly when x⊤Ax≥0x^\top Ax\ge0x⊤Ax≥0 for all xxx, which holds exactly when every eigenvalue is non-negative, and also exactly when A=B⊤BA=B^\top BA=B⊤B for some matrix BBB;
  • AAA is positive definite exactly when x⊤Ax>0x^\top Ax>0x⊤Ax>0 for every x≠0x\neq\mathbf 0x=0, that is, when every eigenvalue is positive;
  • det⁡A>0\det A>0detA>0 alone does not guarantee PSD: diag⁡(−1,−1)\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1)diag(−1,−1) has determinant 111. (In 2024 MCQ 22, statements (a), (b) and (c) are true and (d) is false.)
  • Gram matrices are PSD, since v⊤X⊤Xv=∥Xv∥2≥0v^\top X^\top Xv=\|Xv\|^2\ge0v⊤X⊤Xv=∥Xv∥2≥0; this is the "bowl" of least squares, and adding λI\lambda IλI in ridge regression makes it positive definite.

The singular value decomposition (SVD). Every matrix A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n, of any shape, can be factored as
A=UΣV⊤,A=U\Sigma V^\top ,A=UΣV⊤,
where U∈Rm×mU\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}U∈Rm×m and V∈Rn×nV\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}V∈Rn×n are orthogonal and Σ∈Rm×n\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}Σ∈Rm×n is diagonal, holding the singular values σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥0\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge0σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥0.

  • The link with the EVD. From the factorisation,
    A⊤A=V Σ⊤Σ V⊤,AA⊤=U ΣΣ⊤ U⊤,A^\top A=V\,\Sigma^\top\Sigma\,V^\top,\qquad AA^\top=U\,\Sigma\Sigma^\top\,U^\top ,A⊤A=VΣ⊤ΣV⊤,AA⊤=UΣΣ⊤U⊤,
    so the columns of VVV (the right singular vectors) are eigenvectors of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A, the columns of UUU (the left singular vectors) are eigenvectors of AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤, and σi=λi(A⊤A)\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i(A^\top A)}σi​=λi​(A⊤A)​. Moreover Avi=σiuiAv_i=\sigma_iu_iAvi​=σi​ui​.
  • The geometry. V⊤V^\topV⊤ rotates or reflects in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn; Σ\SigmaΣ scales (and pads or projects when m≠nm\neq nm=n); UUU rotates or reflects in Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm. The unit circle is mapped to an ellipse with semi-axes σiui\sigma_iu_iσi​ui​, and the right singular vectors give the corresponding input directions.
  • Determinants. det⁡(A⊤A)=∏iσi2\det(A^\top A)=\prod_i\sigma_i^2det(A⊤A)=∏i​σi2​. With σ=(6,3,2)\sigma=(6,3,2)σ=(6,3,2) this is 36⋅9⋅4=129636\cdot9\cdot4=129636⋅9⋅4=1296 (2025 MCQ 9); with σ=(5,3,1)\sigma=(5,3,1)σ=(5,3,1) it is 225225225 (2024 MCQ 24).
  • Low-rank approximation (the Eckart–Young theorem). Among all matrices of rank kkk,
    Ak=∑i=1kσi uivi⊤minimises∥A−Ak∥F,and∥A−Ak∥F2=∑i>kσi2.A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i\,u_iv_i^\top \qquad\text{minimises}\qquad \|A-A_k\|_F,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 .Ak​=i=1∑k​σi​ui​vi⊤​minimises∥A−Ak​∥F​,and∥A−Ak​∥F2​=i>k∑​σi2​.
    Storing AkA_kAk​ costs mk+k+knmk+k+knmk+k+kn numbers. In the 2025 Mid, Problem 1, a 2048×15362048\times15362048×1536 image of rank 808080 needs
    2048⋅80+80+80⋅1536=163 840+80+122 880=286 8002048\cdot80+80+80\cdot1536=163\,840+80+122\,880=286\,8002048⋅80+80+80⋅1536=163840+80+122880=286800
    numbers instead of 3 145 7283\,145\,7283145728, a saving of 90.88%90.88\%90.88%; in the 2024 Mid, a 1920×10801920\times10801920×1080 image with k=120k=120k=120 needs 360 120360\,120360120 instead of 2 073 6002\,073\,6002073600, a saving of 82.64%82.64\%82.64%.
  • The best rank-one approximation is B1=σ1u1v1⊤B_1=\sigma_1u_1v_1^\topB1​=σ1​u1​v1⊤​. In the 2025 Mid, Problem 10, with σ1=5\sigma_1=5σ1​=5, u1=12(1,1,0)u_1=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,1,0)u1​=2​1​(1,1,0) and v1=(1,0)v_1=(1,0)v1​=(1,0),
    B1=5⋅12[110][10]=[5/205/2000],B_1=5\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5/\sqrt2&0\\5/\sqrt2&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},B1​=5⋅2​1​​110​​[1​0​]=​5/2​5/2​0​000​​,
    and the eigenvalues of B⊤BB^\top BB⊤B are σ12=25\sigma_1^2=25σ12​=25 and σ22=4\sigma_2^2=4σ22​=4.
  • PCA keeps the top kkk principal components, those with the largest eigenvalues of the covariance matrix; projecting onto them minimises the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ reconstruction error, and discarding the small components reduces noise and redundancy.

Remember: The one line for this lecture

Eigenvectors are the directions a square matrix only scales; stacking them gives A=QΛQ−1A=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}A=QΛQ−1 — change basis, scale, change back — from which det⁡A=∏iλi\det A=\prod_i\lambda_idetA=∏i​λi​, and A−1A^{-1}A−1 and AkA^kAk simply act on the eigenvalues; a zero eigenvalue means dependent columns; and symmetric matrices are the best case, A=QΛQ⊤A=Q\Lambda Q^\topA=QΛQ⊤, with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors.
